headline: Federal bid to revisit Revolution Wind permit puts Connecticut project back in court
dek: The Interior Department wants a judge to send the project’s three-year-old approval back for review even as the nearly completed wind farm is already supplying power to New England.
body: The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to send the approval for Revolution Wind back to the Interior Department for another review, reopening a fight over Connecticut’s first offshore wind project as the 65-turbine farm nears full operation. The request does not itself cancel the project or order its turbines offline, but it creates a new legal uncertainty around a facility that is already producing electricity for the regional grid.

The Department of Justice made the request in a Friday, Oct. 9, filing in a lawsuit brought by Green Oceans, a Rhode Island-based group that challenges federal approvals for Revolution Wind and the South Fork Wind project. [CT Mirror reported](https://ctmirror.org/2026/10/13/trump-administration-seeks-to-rescind-approval-for-revolution-wind/) that Interior is seeking remand of the project’s construction and operations plan approval so the agency can reevaluate whether its review complied with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. Remand would return the approval to the agency for further consideration; it is not the same as a final court ruling that the project’s permit is invalid.

Connecticut officials responded Wednesday by saying the filing conflicts with the administration’s stated interest in faster energy permitting. In an [official statement](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-on-trump-administration-attempt-to-block-new-energy-sources), Gov. Ned Lamont, Attorney General William Tong and DEEP Acting Commissioner Emma Cimino said they were reviewing their options with project developer Ørsted. Tong said the state would be prepared to return to court to protect Connecticut jobs and access to the project’s power.

The dispute is significant because Revolution Wind is no longer only a proposal. The [Connecticut governor’s office](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/10-2026/governor-lamont-on-trump-administration-attempt-to-block-new-energy-sources) says the 704-megawatt project is about 15 nautical miles southeast of Point Judith, Rhode Island, began construction in 2023 and received its 65th and final turbine in September. The project has begun supplying power, and state officials expect full commercial operation later this year. Ørsted’s onshore assembly work has used the State Pier in New London, tying the federal dispute to Connecticut’s port, construction workforce and power customers even though the turbines stand offshore.

At full output, the project is expected to generate enough electricity for about 350,000 homes across New England. Connecticut is contracted to receive 304 megawatts, while Rhode Island is set to receive the remaining 400 megawatts, according to the state release. Connecticut officials say the state’s share would cover about 5% of its electricity demand. DEEP estimates that, by 2028, the project could reduce electricity-market costs for Connecticut and New England ratepayers by roughly $500 million a year and save Connecticut customers $150 million to $200 million in public-benefit charges over the contract’s 20-year life. Those are agency estimates, not guaranteed savings, and depend on the project reaching the expected operating schedule.

The latest filing follows earlier attempts to stop construction. A federal judge allowed work to resume after the administration issued stop-work orders tied to national-security concerns, and the [Sabin Center’s case summary](https://www.climatecasechart.com/collections/revolution-wind-llc-v-burgum%5F6ce6) records that the court granted preliminary relief to the developer and the states in January. The new request instead focuses on whether the original construction-and-operations-plan review adequately addressed the federal law governing uses of the outer continental shelf, according to CT Mirror and [Canary Media’s account of the filing](https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/offshore-wind/trump-reevaluate-permit-revolution-wind-orsted).

Canary Media reported that the filing does not immediately change the project’s construction or generation while the judge considers the request. The court could reject the remand, allow the agency to reconsider the approval, or set additional briefing and conditions; the timing and eventual outcome remain unresolved. The Interior Department told CT Mirror that it was following a briefing schedule and said the filing should not be read as a policy change, while Connecticut’s officials argue that reopening an approval after construction is nearly complete undermines the certainty needed for major energy infrastructure.

For New England, the next concrete step is a decision from U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth in the District of Columbia case. Until then, Revolution Wind remains a permitted, nearly completed project with power already reaching the grid, but its final transition to full commercial operation is proceeding under a fresh legal challenge. The state’s response also signals that Connecticut may again ask the court to protect the project if the federal review threatens the construction schedule, the contracted electricity or the economic benefits officials associate with the wind farm.
location: State Pier, New London, Connecticut, and offshore south of Rhode Island
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Revolution Wind permit review puts Connecticut project back in court
seoDescription: The Interior Department wants a federal judge to reconsider approval of Revolution Wind as the nearly completed offshore project supplies New England power.
